items.title: Mr C, Miami — MBDS
items.text: Miami Mr. C Capturing the timeless charm of Italy’s iconic coastal style, Mr. C Coconut Grove is an elegant and glamorous destination evoking Italy’s golden era from the Cipriani family. The interiors have been inspired by the honesty and materiality of a classic yacht. Martin Brudnizki Bellini Restaurant and Bar sits on the fifth floor of the hotel with floor to ceiling windows taking in the views across Coconut Grove Harbour and the ocean beyond. Anchoring the space to its location, a terrazzo floor spreads across both areas and elegantly combines with the high gloss limed oak panelling and bar. Nautical elements mix with typically Venetian design, as a blue and white stripe features on the seating throughout the scheme, while above sit Murano glass chandeliers – ultimately channelling the feeling of a stylish Italian yacht. Vintage Coastal Luxury Mr. C embodies Italy's golden era charm with yacht-inspired, mid-century interiors and elegant glamour. Selected works

items.title: The Surrey, New York — MBDS
items.text: NEW YORK The Surrey Echoing the heritage of the Upper East Side, The Surrey combines Art Deco with contemporary design to offer timeless elegance. Originally built in 1926, The Surrey has long stood as one of the great addresses of the Upper East Side, renowned for its refined character and quiet sophistication. Reopening in 2024 as Corinthia Hotels’ first property in the US, the hotel enters a new chapter, its design thoughtfully reimagined to reflect both its storied past and the spirit of modern New York. MBDS reimagines the hotel’s rooms, suites, spa, and public areas, bringing a layered and nuanced approach to the interiors. Sumptuous materials and finely crafted details honour the building’s heritage while introducing a fresh, modern expression. The Surrey’s interiors strike a careful balance between a welcoming, residential spirit and a reverence for the building’s architectural heritage. At its core is the idea of ‘sublime comfort’ , a design philosophy that creates a sense of ease and belonging for every guest. History and modernity converge to shape a distinct expression of luxury, one that reflects the Corinthia ethos while capturing the Upper East Side’s refined charm. Through a blend of rich materials and a contemporary classic layered style, the hotel has an atmosphere that feels both refined and residential. MARTIN BRUDNIZKI The hotel’s four signature suites are inspired by the bridges of nearby Central Park. Each suite features bespoke crown mouldings that echo the character of a different bridge, paired with hand-painted illustrations inside the armoire, creating a dialogue between craftsmanship and place. The Surrey Spa is a serene retreat wrapped in marble, where soft curves and a warm, neutral palette create an enveloping sense of calm. Designed to echo Corinthia’s world-renowned approach to wellness, the space invites guests to pause, restore, and emerge renewed - a quiet counterpoint to the energy of the Upper East Side. CASA CODY PALM SPRINGS, CA, 2021 CASA CODY PALM SPRINGS, CA, 2021 photography by Lance Gerber & Josh Cho Inspired by coastal Spain, we composed a rich palette of color & texture to complement the existing historical character of Casa Cody. Casa Cody is the oldest operating hotel in Palm Springs, founded in the 1920s by Hollywood pioneer Harriet Cody, cousin to the legendary Buffalo Bill. The project blends historic preservation with fresh and modern colors, textures and patterns, honoring its Spanish Colonial Revival heritage and adobe hacienda architecture with a new lens. Quiet and secluded yet just steps from Palm Springs’ center, Casa Cody is a romantic respite with 29 rooms including three free-standing accommodations across well-manicured grounds, situated in front of the rising backdrop of the San Jacinto Mountains under the open skies of the California desert. Casa Cody is a designated Class I Historic Site, Palm Springs’ highest level of historic preservation protection. In the early 1900s, Harriet and Harold Bryant Cody came by wagon from Hollywood to Palm Springs where they settled on land that was to become Casa Cody and built a home. With warm coral velvet, textured blue-green accents, and otomi-patterned pillows, the rooms are imbued with depth to enliven the existing plaster interior. Each room features richly colored zellige tile and deep blue millwork in the bathrooms and bar areas, reflecting the Mediterranean influence in a modern design. We custom designed upholstered elements and cabinetry in the space for an inviting, residential feel. Dark wood tones balance the rich pops of color, creating a classic yet modern aesthetic that is unlike any other in Palm Springs, as unique as the vibrant history of the property. With multiple courtyards and spacious lawns against a serene mountain backdrop, Casa Cody is a sanctuary within the creative bustle of downtown Palm Springs. HOTEL LUCILE HOTEL LUCILE Photography By: Chase Daniel Set within a reimagined 1931 Presbyterian church in Silver Lake, Hotel Lucile transforms a historic place of gathering into a 25 key boutique hotel with a bar, restaurant, rooftop garden, and pool. The project approaches the existing structure with a sense of reverence and reinvention, preserving its architectural integrity while introducing a new layer of social and cultural life. The design draws from the language of the church itself, informed by the spirit of Peggy Guggenheim, the consummate collector. Conceived as the European home of an eccentric, well traveled hostess, the hotel unfolds as a series of curated spaces where art, furnishings, and objects feel accumulated over time. Historic materials and finishes remain foundational, while contemporary interventions introduce warmth, intimacy, and a lived in sophistication. The lobby is marked by the building’s original monumental wood entry doors, opening into interiors where plasterwork, moulding, and stained glass have been carefully preserved. These elements establish a rich architectural backdrop that anchors the project in its past while allowing new insertions to feel both intentional and effortless. The experience is lively and layered, forming an energetic threshold between the city and the interior. Dark millwork and preserved detailing ground the space, while the stair becomes an animated moment of color, light, and art. A rotating, shoppable art program curated in collaboration with Rhett Baruch Gallery is integrated throughout, inviting guests to engage with the work as part of the hotel’s evolving narrative. At the heart of the hotel, the former sanctuary has been transformed into a restaurant and bar that retains the dramatic volume and proportions of the original church. Stained glass windows filter light across original wood floors, preserving the spatial hierarchy. The altar has been reimagined as a flexible private dining room, and the choir loft now serves as an intimate lounge. Each intervention honors the history of the space while adapting it for contemporary use. Original stained glass windows depict the lives of saints, casting a layered ambient glow across the space. Beneath them, low-slung custom furnishings and rich, saturated tones create a sensual, lounge-like atmosphere that contrasts with the building’s historic scale. The result is a dynamic social core that feels both reverent and indulgent, where past and present are held in constant dialogue. “Lively, singular, and stylish, public spaces would beckon neighborhood creatives and visitors alike.” – Architectural Digest Each room feels intimate and personal, shaped by proportion, light, and an understated approach to luxury. Arched openings, dark wood built-ins, and tailored upholstery nod to the hotel’s European design cues. Parquet wood floors and soft plaster walls provide a historical backdrop for curated artwork and objects that feel collected over time. “From the beginning, we thought about it as almost an exhibition space, with this European villa feel, like you’re coming into a gallerist’s home,” – Lucia The bathrooms are defined by a layered, tactile material palette. Console sinks feature marble countertops, brass legs, exposed plumbing, and wall mounted fittings that reference traditional washstands. Deep green glazed tile introduces saturated contrast, while custom mosaic floors extend throughout, adding intricacy and variation underfoot. Each space balances richness with warmth, where historic cues are refined through careful detailing and an elevated yet understated approach. Outdoor spaces extend the atmosphere of the hotel into the open air, offering a series of intimate, garden like settings. At the pool, brick paving, lush planting, and tailored lounge seating create a warm, relaxed environment that feels both social and composed. The rooftop garden frames views of Silver Lake and the church tower, pairing striped banquettes and wrought metal furnishings with a softer landscape edge. Together, these spaces carry forward the project’s sensibility, blending hospitality with a relaxed, outdoor way of living. Hotel Lucile brings new life to a historic structure, transforming a once singular place of gathering into a layered and evolving social environment. Through a careful balance of preservation and reinvention, the project bridges past and present, creating spaces that feel rooted, intimate, and distinctly contemporary. items.title: Straker's New York
items.text: Straker's New York Post Company Straker's 2026 New York, NY Food & Beverage Role Interior Design Scope Renovation: Restaurant and Bar Partners Client: Straker's Photogapher: Billal Taright Project Narrative For years, 59 Grand Street was Lucky Strike, one of the rooms that defined downtown dining in SoHo. It is now the first home outside London for Straker’s, chef Thomas Straker’s wood-fired restaurant from Notting Hill, and something of a homecoming for a chef born in the United States. Our renovation keeps the bones of the old institution and treats them as a classic neighborhood restaurant, with a brighter, more natural palette. The room is built around an expansive open kitchen clad in steel and topped in green stone, and its fire and energy reach every corner. At the front, the bar and low banquettes in vegetable-tanned leather look straight into the kitchen. At the back, a dining room set with white tablecloths is more formal, for long dinners and larger gatherings. Work by Keith Haring, Damien Hirst, Brian Clarke and Jake Clark hangs throughout. The same playfulness reaches the bathrooms, which are wrapped floor to ceiling in marble and mirror.

items.title: Bavel — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Bavel Middle Eastern restaurants have long suffered from cliché in design aesthetics such as having a very dark, heavily patterned and often intimidating environments. The design for Bavel set out to challenge those conventions. The restaurant design embraces the influence of the regions from which the cuisine is derived (the southern Mediterranean), interpreting those ideas through the lens of its Arts District location. The worn, rather innocuous brick warehouse which houses the space, served as a wonderfully textured canvas for the restaurant to evolve from. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Los Angeles, CA YEAR 2018 CLIENT Ori Menashe & Genevieve Gergis SIZE 7,200 sq. ft. interior “ In a world of excess and heaviness, this light-filled industrial space adorned with ivy is refreshing. This is handsome and well-done. ” Awards Jury Contract Magazine Natural light served as the critical ingredient employed to create a bright and inviting atmosphere. The center piece of the design is an extensive raceway of planters which hang just below the massive skylight openings, with greenery spilling over and filling the voluminous ceiling area. The primary base color in the space is white with pops of color found in tile, plaster and furnishings that are drawn from the Coastal Mediterranean-vibrant turquoise, saffron and turmeric, and patterns evoking a Moorish feel are found throughout. Seating diversity is plentiful, with a focus on comfort so diners can relax and enjoy, whether inside or on the patio. Modern and traditional styles blend to find the perfect note and finishing touch to the space.

items.title: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
items.text: Dan Howarth 3 October 2026 Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York ‘s Rockefeller Plaza to emulate “a stateroom on an ocean liner”. The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era’s blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. “Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough,” said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city’s dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. “Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York’s layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center,” said INC’s Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel’s five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. On the roof, a bar references the dining rooms of Chinatown via a tomato-red counter framed by tiled portals, temple-like joinery and hand-painted lotus motifs. The Kimpton Era’s guest rooms are designed like compact ship cabins, with each “berth” featuring full white-oak walls that integrate a bed, desk and storage into a single furniture element. White oak millwork integrates multiple furniture pieces in the guest rooms Neutral colour palettes are offset by jewel-toned fabrics and brass accents, while wet-room-style bathrooms are defined by frosted, blackened metal-framed sliding glass doors that conserve space. “[The Kimpton Era] is a self-contained voyage where guest rooms are like staterooms and lounges, and dining rooms unfold like the salons of a great ocean liner in a new expression of New York luxury,” said INC’s Louisa Revitte. Jewel-toned fabrics enliven the otherwise neutral rooms INC’s previous hotel projects have included the 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with Marvel Architects, and the event spaces at the TWA Hotel inside Eero Saarinen’s JFK Airport terminal. The studio – which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year – has also completed “gritty yet inviting” interiors for a restaurant in BIG’s The Spiral skyscraper, and filled its own concrete-forward offices with eclectic furniture and plants. The photography is by Read McKendree . Read more Interiors USA Hotels New York City Midtown Manhattan New York INC Architecture & Design Exclusives

items.title: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 19 October 2026 Photography by Piercarlo Quecchia (unless stated otherwise) Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna’s iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan’s Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Photo by T-Space The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. “By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club,” said Zorzi. “The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions.” At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Photo by T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a “raw” interior for Milan’s Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it’s like to be a contemporary designer in Italy’s design capital. Photography by Piercarlo Quecchia (unless stated otherwise) Read more Italy Milan Bars Stainless steel Listening bars NM3 Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books
items.text: Dan Howarth 31 October 2026 Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) The vintage bookstores of Mexico City ‘s Roma neighbourhood influenced the interiors of this basement bar , designed by local outfit Em-Estudio. Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops. Photo by Rene Villaseñor “It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio . Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond. “The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio. Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere. The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room. Cove lighting illuminates the books, creating a dramatic contrast with the otherwise shadowy bar, while banquettes below are accompanied by circular marble tables for placing drinks. “The pages of thousands of books resting on bookshelves that reach the ceiling shed their literal meaning, becoming a tapestry in shades of white that only time can give, bathed in a gradient of warm light,” Em-Estudio said. Other areas such as the DJ booth, the bar and the bathrooms are highlighted with gold leaf and brass to draw the eye. A further hidden lounge space is disguised by another bookshelf, decorated with cans and objects that “evoke a grocery-store bar”. This room swaps burgundy for green, applied in gloss across the ceiling and appearing in a long marble table that runs through the centre. Dark wood Van Beuren chairs with yellow upholstery are lined up along each side, parallel to more walls of books that are uplit along each shelf. A mirror that covers the back wall visually doubles the space, extending the table and the bookshelves in the reflection. Em-Estudio was co-founded by architect Ivan Esqueda and interior designer Gala Sánchez-Renero – a husband and wife who also operate individual practices. Their previous collaborations include a holiday home on a steep hillside in Oaxaca, Mexico, built from coloured concrete chosen to blend into the rocky mountainside. Project credits: Architecture and interior design: Taller Ivan Esqueda and Gala Sánchez-Renero Estudio Design team: Berenice Galindo, Sergio Peláez, Fabián Cedillo Construction and installations: Miguel Ángel Márquez Carpentry: Leonardo Cabrera Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) Read more Interiors Mexico City Mexico Bars Speakeasies Exclusives

items.title: "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona bar
items.text: Alyn Griffiths 28 June 2026 Spanish designer Isern Serra has completed a speakeasy bar in Barcelona featuring multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton ‘s retro-futuristic 1960s installations. Focacha is the latest venue from hospitality specialist Grupo La Confitería, which tasked Serra ‘s studio with creating a space that pays tribute to an important period in the history of Barcelona’s nightlife. Isern Serra has designed a Barcelona bar with multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton pieces The 1960s and early 1970s coincided with the heyday of Tuset Street where the bar is located, which became a hub for a group of young liberal professionals known in Barcelona art the “gauche divine”. The cocktail bar was designed to evoke the futuristic styling that characterised this time and immerse guests in a multi-sensory environment defined by design, light and music. The bar is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria “I wanted visitors to feel enveloped by an environment with a strong artistic and emotional presence, capable of sparking curiosity and creating a sense of wonder from the very first moment,” Serra told Dezeen. “More than designing a cocktail bar, the intention was to create a setting that evokes emotions, encourages contemplation and leaves a lasting impression on those who experience it, turning their visit into something truly memorable.” Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop The speakeasy-style venue is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria that has been serving Italian bread for 50 years. Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop, which adds a sense of theatricality to the experience. The venue was divided into two spaces, the first of which is a bar that pays homage to Danish designer Panton’s iconic Visiona installations. A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space, forming intimate niches for small groups along one side. On the other side of the space, a stainless-steel bar with rounded edges subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room. The fully carpeted ceiling and walls extend behind the bar, where rounded openings accommodate shelves displaying bottles. A stainless-steel bar subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room “We were inspired by Panton because his creative language perfectly reflects the optimistic, experimental and progressive spirit of the late 1960s and early 1970s,” Serra pointed out. “The goal was not to recreate a retro aesthetic, but to capture the sense of freedom, creativity and innovation that defined that era.” The DJ room was lined with curved banquettes A circular opening at the end of the bar leads into a DJ room designed to merge 1960s nostalgia with a dystopian vision of the future, resulting in a surreal, technology-led aesthetic. The room is lined with curved banquettes that evoke the era’s psychedelic and modular interiors, while the domed ceiling and walls incorporate openings that allow dynamic lighting effects to transform the atmosphere within the space. Mirrored walls create the illusion of more space, while lighting fixtures including the Panton-designed Flowerpot VP2 and Panthella lamps contribute to a carefully curated atmosphere. According to Serra, the interior’s complex curves demanded a sculptural construction approach that meant elements were not fully defined from the outset and evolved as different solutions were tested using mock-ups and full-scale prototypes. Isern Serra said that the interior’s complex curves demanded a sculptural construction “Rather than building conventional architectural elements,” he said, “we were shaping volumes and forms to create a fluid and immersive spatial experience, where every curve contributed to reinforcing the overall atmosphere of the project.” Serra’s studio is based in the Poblenou neighbourhood of Barcelona, in a space he designed to embody the practice’s values and provide an inspirational working environment. The architect is known for combining contemporary, vibrant and essential forms with Mediterranean influences. Previous projects include a gallery-like apartment renovation and a bakery featuring cave-like walls . Read more Spain Barcelona Bars Colour Isern Serra Interiors Highlights

items.title: Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar
items.text: Alyn Griffiths 18 June 2026 Design studio Golem has completed a subterranean cocktail bar in central London featuring a glossy counter and tactile booths entirely covered in soft red velvet. Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive “Dive’s experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests,” explained Golem founder Ariel André. “The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills.” “Wear and tear is part of the architecture,” he added. “Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies.” The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive’s owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains “the imprint of bodies” “The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus,” André explained. A dark corridor leads to the steps that descend into the richer, more tactile lounge space. This area was designed to facilitate moments of interaction between guests, while also offering cosy corners for private conversations. Structural arches supporting the street above contain flexible seating areas that can be configured to suit various social scenarios. Built-in benches lining the niches are covered with loose cushions that can be repositioned as required. “The upholstery is conceived to be appropriated by guests,” André pointed out. “Bodies shape the furniture, not the other way around.” “When unoccupied, the seating still carries the imprint of previous guests, holding the evening in a suspended time and space.” Golem aimed to create cosy corners for private conversations One of the arches known as the “fun room” is covered from floor to ceiling in lush carpet, allowing its U-shaped layout to be used for anything from lounging to dancing. Golem created quart-de-lune tables specially for the project, which can be used individually by couples sitting side by side, or combined in sets of two or four to comfortably seat up to eight guests. The main bar features contrasting smooth, glossy finishes The lounge also functions as a listening room, with the choice of absorbent and reflective surfaces helping to create a tailored acoustic environment. A dedicated DJ booth is positioned next to bespoke shelves housing the owner’s extensive vinyl collection. The mixing desk is height adjustable to allow for seated or standing performance. A one-way mirror conceals the bathroom At the centre of the bar, the non-gendered bathrooms are arranged around a banquette where guests can sit and chat. A one-way mirror conceals this space from the outside while providing a glimpse back into the lounge. André founded his Paris-based studio in 2021, working across the worlds of architecture, art and design. Previous Golem projects include a modular furniture system made of hundreds of squishy balls , which was used to create a conversation pit in a Brussels apartment. Read more London UK Bars Interiors

items.title: All About Bar Cosme, Enrique Olvera’s Sultry Evening Spot in NoHo — Resy | Right This Way
items.text: All About Bar Cosme, Enrique Olvera’s Sultry Evening Spot in NoHo — Resy | Right This Way Bar Cosme 4.8 · Modern Mexican · $$$ NoHo Book Now Published: Nov. 18, 2026 Chef and restaurant owner Enrique Olvera has had a very busy 2026. His group Casamata debuted San Damián and Ditroit in Southern California, and Pujol.itto in Mexico City. Their final opening for the year is actually a flip, transforming the NoHo space that housed Atla for nearly a decade into Bar Cosme , which opened on Nov. 10. Despite Bar Cosme’s name, this sibling of his Flatiron spot Cosme , is a restaurant, not a bar. “We want people to come in and have dinner, but in a bar experience [at] a counter,” Olvera says. “As we [get to] know ourselves better, we recognize that this is the kind of dining we want to propose. Where you can see the interaction,” he says. A big, open kitchen takes up a large portion of the room, where chefs press and cook tortillas on a rotating comal to order. The presentation here is pared back. “We want to keep things as simple as possible, but very high quality,” Olvera adds. Dinner can be ordered à la carte, but the menu is designed as a $135 prix fixe, where guests choose one item from four sections. Most of the ​mains,​​​ like lamb belly and Dover sole, come largely unadorned and with tortillas on the side. That simplicity is also reflected in the design, which feels moody, sleek, and in situ. Despite the group’s roots in Mexico, Olvera says: “We don’t want the restaurant to feel like it landed from somewhere else. We want to do a New York restaurant with Mexican food.” Here’s everything you need to know about Bar Cosme. The Resy Rundown Bar Cosme Why We Like It Think of Bar Cosme as Cosme’s younger, downtown sister. All of the seating is at two long bars and everything is accompanied by tortillas pressed to order or tostadas. Essential Dishes While diners can order à la carte, the menu is designed as a $135 prix fixe. Start with the king trumpets with duck sabayon or oysters with jicama, then move on to the lamb belly in xintextle, and soft-serve or Cosme’s signature corn husk meringue for dessert. Must-Order Drinks The cocktail menu from Eleven Madison Park vet Sebastian Tollius and Casamata’s Jorsand Diaz is broken into two parts: “De la Casa” for spins on classics like a martini with mezcal-brined morita smoked olives; and “De la Barra” for inventive creations like the Lestat with Tequila, corn, yellow Chartreuse, and passion fruit. Who and What It’s For There are no tables at Bar Cosme; all of the leather stools line two long black granite counters; bring a date or come solo. Reserve a spot facing the kitchen, if you like a show. How to Get In Reservations drop 30 days in advance at 10 a.m. with limited seatings held for walk-ins from 5 to 9 p.m. After 9 p.m., the restaurant is walk-ins only. Pro Tip Every meal here starts with tostadas and two salsas, which change daily. Expect ones like a Thai-inspired salsa with fish sauce and habanero chiles, and a Japanese riff on salsa borracha or “drunken salsa” made with sake instead of pulque. Bar Cosme is located in the NoHo space that housed Atla for nearly a decade, which was entirely overhauled with a focus on looking inwards. Photo by Evan Sung, courtesy of Bar Cosme Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme 1. Corn is served with nearly every dish. “The idea is that you always have some kind of corn preparation,” Olvera explains. Eating here is meant to be a little playful, he adds, with diners using their hands to assemble their perfect bite. The meal kicks off with tostadas and two salsas, which rotate daily, like one that takes inspiration from Thailand with fish sauce blended with habanero chiles, and a Japanese take on salsa borracha, or drunken salsa made with sake instead of pulque. As diners reach the main course, the tostadas are swapped with tortillas that are pressed to order and cooked on a comal in the center of the restaurant that’s so large, it rotates, so the chefs can reach all of the tortillas. “I think tortillas are more and more, for us, the center of the restaurant,” Olvera says. Like the ones at Cosme, the tortillas here are made with heirloom corn varieties from Mexico sourced by suppliers like Masienda. Corn also finds its way onto the dessert. The team is also serving Cosme’s signature dish, the corn husk meringue . The Dover sole. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme The Dover sole. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme 2. The menu is built as a $135 prix fixe, but you can still order à la carte. “When you have a restaurant that wants you to come often, it’s nice to keep things simple,” Olvera says. Milton Revilla , who has worked with the Casamata team for years, is overseeing the kitchen at Bar Cosme. The menu is divided into four sections including starters to pair with those tostadas like prawn tartare with prawn head mayonnaise and king trumpets with duck sabayone, which is a small nod to the beloved duck carnitas at Cosme. In the 12 years since Olvera opened Cosme, New York’s taco scene has grown exponentially. So there are no assembled tacos on the menu here, by design. The main course offerings focus on proteins adorned primarily with just a sauce like Dover sole al ajillo, with garlic, guajillo chile sliced almost as finely as saffron threads, and olive oil. There’s also lamb belly in xintextle , a sauce traditionally made with dried shrimp, which the team swapped for a variety of toasted and crushed ants that taste like beef jerky. Sides like those at a steakhouse can be mixed and matched with the proteins. There’s roasted onion in salsa matcha, potato puree , and a chicory and radish salad . Diners can order à la carte, but the portions will be more substantial. Instead of a piece of the Dover sole, expect a whole fish. The small dessert selection includes soft-serve and an affogato with espresso made with beans from La Cabra and an ice cream flavored with the seeds of mamey fruit that tastes ​a bit like​​​ marzipan. The Lestat with tequila, corn, yellow chartreuse, and passion fruit. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme The Lestat with tequila, corn, yellow chartreuse, and passion fruit. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme 3. The creative cocktail menu borrows ingredients from the kitchen. Designed by ​beverage directors Jorsand Diaz and Sebastian Tollius , an Eleven Madison Park alum, the cocktail menu is divided in two sections: De la Casa, which are classics like margaritas, martinis, and Manhattans reimagined with a Mexican flare, and De la Barra, which are more inventive drinks. “We didn’t want to just throw classic drinks on there without our personal touch,” Tollius says. The martini (gin or vodka) comes with mezcal-brined morita smoked olives. Meanwhile, the Manhattan at Bar Cosme is made with cacao husks and pasilla mixe, a prized smoky chile. With the De la Barra cocktails, the team really ran with their creativity, creating drinks like the Lestat , which has a tropical touch. It’s made from tequila, corn, yellow chartreuse, and passion fruit. The Silas is their take on the Mexican after dinner drink, a carajillo, and an espresso martini. Both reposado and añejo tequila are fat washed with brown butter for nuttiness and mixed with sherry, Licor 43, ​amontillado, ​and ​coffee​​​. It’s frothy, slightly dry and lightly sweet, Tollius says. The wine list, which offers a large selection by the glass, takes a “philosophy first” approach, Diaz explains. “We work with very niche producers that focus a lot on terroir, their farming practices, [and] minimal intervention.” They looked for wines with acidity and structure to stand up to the kitchen’s spicy cooking like Vinos Pijoan’s Árbol de Fuego , an unfiltered rosé from Valle de Guadalupe in Mexico. items.title: Jaç HiFI Café — Openhouse Magazine
items.text: Jaç HiFI Café — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design Jaç HiFI Café A 21st century temple of sound Photographed by Salva López Written by Openhouse Studio Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share A new café has taken over Avinguda Diagonal 335, in the heart of Barcelona: JAÇ HiFi Café. Designed by Isern Serra Studio , the space opened in July 2025 with not one, but two missions: to invite guests to drink coffee and to listen. In fact, its name carries multiple meanings: a nod to jazz music itself, a reference to Japan’s jazz kissa and in Catalan, the word “jaç,” which means to recline, rest, and let go. But, what were jazz kissa ? Characterized by compact and dimly lit venues, these spaces were intimate listening bars that flourished from the 1950s onwards and were dedicated entirely to the appreciation of recorded jazz. Its complex nature, designed and conceived as temples of sound, found no similarities elsewhere: they were neither bars in the Western sense nor cafés in the European style. Close Instead, in jazz kissa , conversation was minimal, the record player was sacred, and music was played on high-fidelity equipment at volumes that demanded full attention. Originating after the Second World War, kissa provided a haven for serious listeners who could not afford records or audio systems of their own. Over decades, their interiors developed a distinct aesthetic — wood-panelled walls, warm lighting, and seating arranged to face the speakers rather than each other — creating a sense of intimacy and deep focus. Close JAÇ HiFi Café reinterprets that philosophy for a contemporary Mediterranean city. The design is warm yet refined, with an emphasis on tactile materials and an atmosphere that feels as familiar as one’s own living room. The space, covering 95 square metres, unfolds in a series of distinct zones, each offering a different relationship with music, people, and the city outside. Close In the lounge area, iconic pieces such as Akari E lamp by Isamu Noguchi and artwork by artist Chidy Wayne welcome the visitors. Further into the bar, a monolithic piece of walnut wood that doubles as a giant speaker cabinet plays both parts, as a functional counter and audio sculpture. The most dramatic element of JAÇ, however, lies toward the rear: a large walnut-wood installation that curves across walls and ceiling to form a semi-enclosed listening alcove. The effect is immersive — a space that seems to embrace the listener, pulling them into a cocoon of warm wood and resonant sound. Close Overall, JAÇ conveys a special closeness, brought by its design and enhanced by the music and the people that enjoy it. With contrasting but matching materials, the space is given its own unique personality, bridging Japanese precision with Mediterranean ease. All accompanied by lighting, shaping the atmosphere and framing shared moments. JAÇ HiFi Café ultimately reimagines the jazz kissa experience for 21st-century Barcelona. It offers a place to slow down, to sit alone or with friends, to discover a song or hear an old favourite in new detail, and to inhabit a space where design, music, and human presence are in perfect balance. items.title: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 6 October 2026 Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry . Located in the city’s Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Arcane 17 is a Basque and Catalan restaurant Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners’ Catalan roots through their restaurant design. “Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language,” studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen. Bétyle Studio designed the interiors for the space In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood. The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster. Classic bentwood chairs make up the dining space “We drew inspiration from the energy of rural churches, dark woods and the movement of traditional fans,” explained Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. “We did not want these references to be literal, but rather to emerge through materials, textures and forms.” Classic, bentwood chairs feature alongside uniform timber tables. In one corner, a red-clad banquette subtly nods to traditional Parisian bistros. All of the space’s joinery was conceived bespoke for the restaurant by a Marseille-based carpenter and frequent collaborator of Bétyle Studio. “We worked with different species of wood and experimented with various techniques to stain, ebonise and patinate the timber,” said Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. “The idea was to give depth to the surfaces and create elements that feel as though they could have belonged to the space for a long time.” Playful marquetry was created specifically for the project Local studio Côme Clérino designed a selection of chunky plaster sconces specifically for the restaurant that loosely resemble elongated seashells. Founded in January 2025, Bétyle Studio works across interior architecture and furniture design. Last year, the studio transformed an old farm building in Marseille into a compact, wood-lined home. Elsewhere in Paris, architect Cyrus Ardalan recently renovated a corner apartment with a timber-heavy interior, complete with porthole-style openings designed to feel nautical. The photography is by Axel Aurejac . Read more France Paris Wood Restaurants Renovations Marquetry Bétyle Studio Interiors
